props.title: One A.M.
props.initialSlug: Charlie Chaplin stumbles home drunk in solo comedy

sections.content: **One A.M.** (1916) stands as one of Charlie Chaplin's most innovative solo performances, where he essentially creates a one-man show battling inanimate objects. Unlike his other shorts like The Pawnshop (1916) or **The Rink** (1916), this film strips away supporting characters to focus purely on physical comedy. Chaplin plays a wealthy drunk attempting to navigate his house after returning home at 1 AM, turning everyday objects like a rotating table, stuffed animal, and Murphy bed into formidable adversaries. The film showcases Chaplin's masterful slapstick timing without relying on his usual character relationships.

sections.content: The film's innovative approach to solo performance influenced later physical comedians, particularly in how it transformed domestic spaces into obstacle courses. **Buster Keaton's** One Week (1920) similarly battled with an uncooperative house, while **Harold Lloyd's** Safety Last! (1923) took the concept vertical with his famous building climb. **One A.M.** demonstrates how early cinema could create compelling entertainment with minimal elements - just one performer and a set full of props. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation in Early Comedy

Chaplin's camera work in **One A.M.** (1916) was surprisingly sophisticated for its era. While most contemporary comedies used static wide shots, Chaplin employed tracking shots to follow his drunken stumbling and clever angles to emphasize the mounting absurdity of his predicament. This technical sophistication would influence later silent comedies like **The Navigator** (1924) and **The General** (1926), where Keaton expanded on the concept of man versus environment.
